meta.title: Surviving Code Reviews in the era of AI
meta.author: mrpossoms
meta.body:
My coworkers are all fully AI pilled. As a consequence, every PR that comes my way for review is on average ~6k lines of diff.

It's well established that even PRs an order of magnitude smaller than this are too big to be effectively reviewed. I'm still clinging to the idea that us humans should understand how the systems we are building work, so I'm hesitant to use AI for reviews aside from more general question answering. Much of what it produces in the way of explanations are difficult to follow and overly verbose anyway.

I'm sure I'm not the only person here who has been dealing with this problem, so I'm curious if anyone here has found any strategies (organizational or personal) which have helped weather this maelstrom.

comments.author: wmoxam
comments.text:
6k diffs are completely unreviewable, and would be rejected in our workplace. We have rules that PRs with diffs cannot be > 400 lines (with exceptions for things like moving code).  These rules apply if the code is produced by AI or humans, there is no difference between the two.

We use AI PR reviews, but only as a first pass in order to save human reviewers some time.

IMO AI tools are useful but they are just that, tools. The code produced and decisions made are still the responsibility of the people using the tools. Ex: AI isn't capable of deciding if code is good enough to ship.

comments.author: bmo
comments.text: I imagine that many of us are finding ourselves in the position that large PRs should be unacceptable and can't possibly be reviewed effectively, but we have no political will to actually enforce that. Management wants things to go out and cares less how you feel about it. So the choice is to either give up and let it through, or become a point of friction for everyone that will eventually have a target on their back. I would love to keep the standards high and just use AI as a tool to make it easier to meet them, but it's not what I'm seeing on the ground.

comments.author: x64k
comments.text:
This might be controversial but at some point it's just not in my job description to rescue someone else's company from their own misguided ideas or from their failure to promote people who understand engineering quality management.

It's not just that it's impossible for a human reviewer to productively review a 6000-line blob (I mean, at least if it were a sequence of commits that you can follow or something...). It's impossible for a human reviewer to productively sit in the loop with a review agent and judge its output in any objective capacity.

Is that a good way to write software? No. Does it produce good software? Also no. Am I going to fret over it and fight for proper engineering quality standards, thus doing the job that's supposedly meant to be done by the people who get multi-million bonuses on bad fiscal years when they fail to meet every single objective, wave the company card for 2,000-dollar dinners, and take two-year sabbaticals? Not until I get my multi-million failure bonus, at least 2K in steaks and tequila, and my two-year sabbatical.

Is it very likely that said software is eventually going to become unmaintainable and the company will eventually crash out? Absolutely -- but my job literally ends at saying so.

comments.author: technomancy
comments.text:
Is it very likely that said software is eventually going to become unmaintainable and the company will eventually crash out?


Not that you're wrong, but the problem is this the entire industry, not a few companies here and there.

comments.author: x64k
comments.text:
I know what you mean. But the need for reliable programmable logic has existed for a few centuries now. I am optimistic that it will continue to exist for a long time now. Either AI tools are going to eventually become good enough that we'll be able to use them to write good software at scale -- not necessarily in terms of vibecoding, but as tools that actually and meaningfully improve our ability to reason about things and write code; or it's going to remain a bubble that will eventually burst and this whole vibe train is going to implode.

I don't really want to bet my professional life on either. The market can stay irrational way longer than I can stay sane, and that works at both ends of the spectrum -- it can block legitimate and potentially successful but less ambitious AI applications while everyone's chasing AGI that can replace real programmers, just like it can continue to lull people who think the hard part of writing good software is that you can't do it in plain English.

It would certainly suck if the software industry were to collapse. And I don't mean that just in selfish terms (although that too, my one other useful trade has gone unpracticed for more than a decade now). But I'm not very inclined to lament its demise. The software industry, broadly speaking, is a few islands of sanity and work that's valuable for society (which I suspect would be able to survive the industry's demise) in a sea of scams and rent-seeking bullshit. I'm going to think about shedding tears for it after I get back from my two-year sabbatical :-).

Edit: I mean... to be clear, I'm not happy about it at all. There's a real chance that, ten years from now, what was once my profession will be a quaint hobby, either because real programmers will be genuinely replaced or (more likely IMHO) because, between collective delusion and some companies being too big to fail, there's just not going to be a place for people who can program in the software industry.

That's still no reason for me to care about someone else's company :). If even the pretense that we're trying to write good software is off and we're switching to full cash grab mode, I'm happy to toe that line for cash and keep writing good software for myself in my spare time.

comments.author: Student
comments.text:
Is that a good way to write software? No. Does it produce good software? Also no.


I don’t think we know this. If you repeatedly prompt Claude to review, and look for simplifications you can get it to produce something pretty good that you can actually read and meaningfully supervise.

comments.author: x64k
comments.text:
I'm sure that if I repeatedly prompt Claude to review and look for simplifications in a 6,000-line PR, it can produce useful review material. But based on how well I can ingest substantially smaller PRs. I'm 100% convinced that whatever I'd be doing would not be meaningful supervision.

I've used LLMs for reviews (fortunately, my employer has a pretty sane AI use policy, so we're not on a token spend hype train). They're useful for orientation and stuff, absolutely, they have made it much easier for me to review code, and I don't just mean I can review more code and faster, I can review it better.

But even Fable falters consistently on much smaller code volumes. No way I could steer it back on track on something that huge.

comments.author: Student
comments.text: It won’t just produce useful review material it will happily make the changes. If you keep doing that you generally can get better, shorter code.

comments.author: x64k
comments.text: How will I know it's better if I can barely tell what it's doing in the first place!?

comments.author: Student
comments.text: Skim on each iteration to give it feedback. Monitor to make sure the diff is getting smaller. Once it basically refuses to come up with changes actually review.

comments.author: x64k
comments.text:
I'm... maybe misunderstanding your point, or we're talking about different things here. I don't understand how that could ever produce anything but a long trail of bugs.

First: the whole starting point is a huge PR that I can't really make sense of. How am I going to "give feedback" and review the changes that the agent makes in response on a diff set that I already don't really understand? I couldn't really review the original PR, and I'm going to fix that by making a bunch of changes to it!?

Second: why am I simplifying code that I may not understand very well, instead of the person who actually wrote it and who hopefully understands it?

Nevermind that I'm now doing someone else's work, but this is literally one of the first things I look for in a review. If the person submitting a PR doesn't understand their code then it's not getting merged period -- they won't be able to make an informed decision about any feedback that I give. It's not that it might be vibecoded, this is a problem as old as programming -- for all I know they pasted the wrong thing off of Stack Overflow/some forum/USENET/the reference manual and it works by accident.

Plus, this raises obvious questions about what I'm actually reviewing at the end of this whole exercise. If I can barely make sense of the original changeset, how am I even going to tell if the "simplified" version is even functionally equivalent?

This is literally worse than where we started from. I'd be reviewing a changeset obtained by starting from a larger changeset that I already didn't understand very well and passing it through a refactoring tool whose output I can't review -- because I couldn't review the original changeset in the first place, let alone changes to that changeset!

comments.author: Student
comments.text: I’m talking about how someone can produce good code using a coding agent, which I thought was the question at issue. The author of the MR should be doing that before they show it to anyone else.

comments.author: x64k
comments.text: Yeah, that explains it -- I was talking about reviewing a MR where the author didn't do that, which is what sparked this whole sub-thread :).

comments.author: olliej
comments.text:
This might be controversial but at some point it's just not in my job description to rescue someone else's company from their own misguided ideas or from their failure to promote people who understand engineering quality management.


I really don't understand what you mean here?

Do you mean random third party devs trying to get you to review patches to an open source project? In which case 100%: no obligation to waste time on garbage PRs produced by the intelligence of a drunk recent and very mediocre graduate.

If it's your own employer: you do have a duty to protect the users of a product you are contributing to. Much like the engineers who failed to prevent Boeing's MCAS from causing a crash are partially responsible for the subsequent deaths (vs. the people who deliberately made and approved the changes have committed murder and should be subject to the penalties).

The correct response is: this PR is not reviewable, and I will not review it. Split it into a reviewable series, please provide a record of your prior review of the code so I am aware of prior issues so that I can make sure I don't miss similar issues.

Also: make sure that there is a written record of this, make reference to your relevant engineering, industry, or (esp. if NGO) government safety rules. Everything must be recorded: email communication, spoken/video communication should be followed by an archivable recap email or similar.

This isn't just about protecting end users or clients of end users, it's about protecting yourself.

comments.author: x64k
comments.text:
So... two things. First, just to set the record straight on ethics: if I worked on something like Boeing's MCAS, yes, absolutely. I would certainly say that the PR is not reviewable. I would work with that person to help them make it reviewable, won't provide a review until then, and if it becomes a point of friction I'm going to friction it to kingdom come. I will sooner resign than rubberstamp something that I think should not be rubberstamped for my users' sake.

This has been my response when working on safety-critical systems pre-AI era. It has always worked in that period. Every time I've worked on something safety-critical, it has been at companies where everyone understood that kind of responsibility, literally up to the board level. There was, I guess, one exception, early-ish in my career, but I resigned over way less than that (tl;dr asked me to lie to a potential customer about my experience).

I haven't done safety-critical work in the LLM era for a bunch of reasons (pandemic, economy and so on) -- I've reluctantly switched career track since then, but I absolutely understand the ethical implications here.

Second: I am obviously not saying that I will happily do this unprompted (no pun intended :-) ).

My normal response would be, yes, this is not reviewable in this form, but let's see what we can do about it. My post is strictly in the context of the post I was replying to:


I imagine that many of us are finding ourselves in the position that large PRs should be unacceptable and can't possibly be reviewed effectively, but we have no political will to actually enforce that. Management wants things to go out and cares less how you feel about it. So the choice is to either give up and let it through, or become a point of friction for everyone that will eventually have a target on their back.


(Emphasis mine)

This impacts all fields of software development, whether safety-critical or not. There's plenty of software that handles no personal data, isn't safety critical, and causes nothing more than some annoyance. So I'm not saying just keep pressing Enter until your avionics firmware is written.

Obviously, my first response would be exactly what you're saying. But if what I get back is escalation up to someone who tells me "run it through Claude and work with that or else", I am going to explain why it's a bad idea once, maybe twice (if I suspect good faith), and then, unless I have a real ethical reason to do otherwise, I am going to run it through Claude and work with that.

So unless the overwhelming being a decent human being duty of not ruining people's lives would demand something else, and as long as I have it in writing that all I can do is watch (for the exact reason you've mentioned), I will very gladly collect my paycheck and watch incompetent management sink a company into the ground.

But, also in order to protect myself, if that overwhelming duty prevails, I'm not going to waste time and energy trying to build real software quality standards by undermining poor software quality management. I will just quit.

You cannot save literally everyone from bad decisions. It sucks and the fact that our society is structured in a way that empowers so many people whose confidence so far exceeds their expertise to make so many bad decisions is part of why it's in such a sad state.

But at the end of the day, if it comes to choosing between hopefully reforming someone else's company from the bottom and working someplace that doesn't have to be reformed, I will take the latter, every single time. For one thing, I'd rather build a better future than keep trying to make this one suck less. And for another, the kind of work that the former choice implies is usually draining to the point where it makes not just my life worse, but the life of everyone around me, too. No one's company is worth that, and as much as it pains me to say it, no stranger's life, either -- that's what regulatory bodies are for.

comments.author: technomancy
comments.text:
Yeah, this is what I've seen at both my current and previous employer. It's an extremely predictable outcome to anyone who was paying attention a couple years ago. Everybody is riding the Vibe Bobsled all the way down the hill: https://dustycloud.org/blog/faulty-towers-vibe-sickness-and-the-vibe-bobsled/

My strategy is to try to keep my head down and try to ride out the bubble. Not at all satisfying, but I don't think there is a better option.

comments.author: sunshowers
comments.text: This is very unfortunate, particularly given LLMs are great at splitting up commits and handling merge conflicts. Any chance you can convince your coworkers to use agents for that? Or is it a lost cause?

comments.author: bmo
comments.text: My feeling right now is lost cause. There's a lack of direction from leadership other than "use AI to go faster." So some amount of people are always going to interpret that as liberally as possible and resist anything that would add friction.

comments.author: sunshowers
comments.text: This is so unfortunate. I feel like I get so much value out of making commits smaller -- I keep finding so many issues in smaller pieces of work (the maxim of larger chunks of work getting less thorough review is very real)

comments.author: gnyeki
comments.text: Do you give the agent a cutoff diff size that it shouldn't go above, or just ask it to split whenever the diff is hard to grasp? What's worked well for you?

comments.author: sunshowers
comments.text: Something that helps me personally is focusing on is refactoring versus functional changes. Even in the before times, the way I liked to build new features was changing the world over a series of commits until until the new feature became inevitable. So my work will sometimes have 10 preparatory refactors, 1 functional change, another 5 refactor commits and then another functional change. Reviewers then can focus their attention on the functional changes.

comments.author: singpolyma
comments.text:
But what does this resistance look like? You refuse to merge the PR because it's garbage. Is your manager coming to threaten firing over that?

I've had people refuse to merge my hand crafted PRs for much more B's reasons than this many times and no one ever ordered them to merge it anyway 😛

comments.author: faassen
comments.text:
Yeah, I was going to say the same thing. I learned that with a tool like jj assisted by AI you can actually make really readable series of commits designed to be reviewable, and that you understand.

That takes time and human attention. AI can not only assist to make more code faster, it can assist in understanding, being more carefully and being more legible as well. The question is whether people and organizations are actually interested in this.

comments.author: wrs
comments.text:
I have been doing some fairly large things successfully by having similar interactions with Claude that I would with a mid-level engineer. I review the plan, ask a lot of probing questions, look for code smells, and make it produce the work as a small set of stacked commits (thanks jj!). (I.e., “Fix this in the original bad commit if possible.”)

I don’t deeply review the code until it’s been through one or two full Claude code-review cycles (which are pretty impressive) and findings are addressed. Then I have it write a review guide to walk me through the code. Then I review the code.

No doubt some would argue that I don’t need to do any of that, but I disagree, based on the stuff that gets fixed in the process.

comments.author: drmorr
comments.text: Are there any actually good AI PR review tools for this sort of "first pass" analysis? I would actually like this if it existed, but every tool I've seen produces absolute dogshit feedback and is OUTRAGEOUSLY expensive

comments.author: sunshowers
comments.text: I use Claude locally with this plugin and this prompt. It is very effective at finding issues.

comments.author: markerz
comments.text:
We use Greptile, after comparing it with CodeRabbit.  From our experience, CodeRabbit was horribly noisy and useless.  Greptile catches a fair number of issues and I strive for a 5/5 rating from it.  Even the false positives are fine because it requires a human to say “no because…” instead of implying it.

Often, I’ll draft a PR, Greptile gives feedback, and I’ll redo the full PR or stack because of something it flagged.  My coworkers get added once the AI reviews are resolved.

comments.author: viraptor
comments.text:
Codex as GH bot (https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/third-party/github) is actually really good this year and many times picked up things I completely missed. Occasionally it's still dumb but then you just downvote that comment and move on. It's definitely worth it.

Overall, make sure you use something that has access to the whole codebase rather than looking just at the patch.

comments.author: koreth
comments.text:
The Codex GH bot has gotten much better at spotting corner cases that require multiple steps lately, in my experience. Just today, on one of my PRs, it correctly pointed out a scenario of the form, "If the user does A, then an admin does B, then the user does C, the rate-limiting code will incorrectly delay the email notification about C," where the B action was something that didn't involve any code I was modifying in the PR.

It does still make a fair number of incorrect or irrelevant comments, but it's now regularly spotting real user-visible bugs before a human reviewer has even looked at the PR.

comments.author: wrs
comments.text: Builtin Claude Code /code-review is pretty darn good in my experience, if you tell it not to limit the output to ten findings (why on earth?) and produce a persistent numbered list of findings you can then walk through and address.

comments.author: wmoxam
comments.text:
We just use Github copilot, I haven't tried anything else. The majority of the feedback is useful IMO.

Honestly I'm not looking for much in a first pass AI review, I just want to know about things like gaps in test coverage for added code, spelling mistakes, etc and have them fixed before a human sees it.

comments.author: jado
comments.text: anyone else constantly reading >5k line PRs? even before AI? this seems exaggerated

comments.author: mosburger
comments.text:
we tried like five or six for a while to compare them all (we didn't have them all looking at the same PR, we created multiple PRs on a single branch for this experiment and assigned different bots to each one) and eventually settled on cubic. For whatever that's worth. Our devex team set up the experiment and got feedback from the engineers on which one seemed the most helpful. I've found cubic to be pretty good tbh.

EDIT because the context probably matters: We have a bunch of medium-sized typescript apps that do a lot of financial computation with a basic React UI bolted on.

comments.author: CharlesT
comments.text:
I have this problem too, and its taken me awhile but the point of view I arrived at is:


i don't waste my time doing work that my boss doesn’t want me to do.


My proclivity is towards careful review and slimming down prs.
My boss has been very clear that he wants only high level review around “is the feature working and are their automated tests “

I’d say if you’re out of step with the rest of the team expectation wise maybe have a sit down with management and figure out what they’re expecting from review.

I would not recommend trying to warn about them of the ills or pitfalls of excessive uncritical AI usage. You are unlikely to convince them with words. The organization has to feel the fallout out of their decision-making to make changes. Naysaying has usually only worsened my credibility.

comments.author: jbauer
comments.text:
This is revealing to you in plain sight the engineering culture at your workplace. If you don't have the agency to reject those PRs and say "I can't reasonably review a 6000 line PR, break it down into smaller changes" then your workplace has a big problem.

People should be understanding what they're committing to a codebase. They should be able to explain to you in their own words what the purpose of a given diff is. If they can't do that and you're expected to not push back, just write "LGTM!", and hit merge, then you're working at a slop company producing slop. This is not responsible use of AI.

Some people (or their managers) can be reasoned with and told "hey, this isn't working, this isn't good engineering, stop this. (etc)" and come back to reality. So see if you can arrange a conversation with your team/manager to get guidelines or rules put in place about people taking ownership of their code, max PR lengths, use of stacked PRs, human-written explanations, etc. Maybe stressing the "we want to be using AI responsibly" point can work.

If you can't talk about this at your workplace—or you do but they don't see a problem and won't change anything—then I'm sorry to say that you're going to have to either put up with it (by not doing reviews at all or ensuring that you're just meeting your manager's expectations like what CharlesT mentioned) or make the tough decision to leave. It sucks, but that's how it goes when you clash with your workplace culture.

TL;DR: talk to your team and managers about it, express your concerns and try to change things for the better. There is no other strategy. There is no fixing this without other people being on board.

comments.author: munificent
comments.text:
I believe going forward, there will be two kinds of software teams:




Ones where there is an expectation that no matter how much AI helps, a human is ultimately responsible for understanding all of the source code and keeping an on eye on it as it evolves. Every line of code landed must go through someone's eyeballs first.

This is how most dedicated software companies have run for the past few decades.




Ones where the software is written and maintained by AI agents. Humans have an executive role over the codebase: they can inspect bits and pieces if they want, but are much more likely to ask AI questions about the code and trust the answer.

This is how most non-software companies who contracted out to a separate development house for their bespoke software has worked for decades. If you're a bakery and you want some custom program to help you keep track of orders and figure out how much of each kind of donut to bake each day, you found a software contracting company and hired them to write you a program. You're a baker, you can't read code. All you could do is ask the company what the program does and trust their answers. The difference now is that instead of it being a separate company of humans, it's a set of AI agents. But the workflow is the same.



Both models are viable and I expect that we will continue to see both styles for many years going forward. I won't make any claims as to which model is better under which conditions.

However, it is absolutely essential that everyone on the team be crystal clear about which development style they're doing or no one is going to be happy. It sounds like you're a #1 and the rest of your team is a #2. You'll need to get that sorted out.

comments.author: wofo
comments.text: Thanks for writing this out! I had a gut feeling in this direction but struggled getting it into words.

comments.author: abeyer
comments.text: What I think this glosses over, though, is that even where the baker operated under model 2, that was just an abstraction over the execution. The development house themselves were still operating under model 1.

comments.author: munificent
comments.text:
The development house themselves were still operating under model 1.


Right, I understand that. But from the baker's perspective, the actual source code and its maintenance is a black box. I think some development teams using AI use the same model. They are no longer really developers. They are more like salespeople at a software contracting business. They talk to the customers, and they talk to the agents writing the code, but they almost never see the code themselves.

comments.author: abeyer
comments.text: Yes, I understand (or at least think I do) what you're saying, and agree there are some "development" teams doing that. However, I still think there's a meaningful difference between a project where someone only has a high-level view of what's happening in model 1 at some lower layer and a project that's just vibes all the way down.

comments.author: mandeep
comments.text:
I think this shape can also vary within an organisation, e.g. depending on the part of the codebase. Product or frontend is more vibe-codeable and vibe-reviewable than an in-house secrets store.

But yes, I agree, and I think clear expectations are important.

comments.author: markerz
comments.text:
Set boundaries and say “no”, with ways to get to “yes”.  I quickly review small PRs and ignore big ones to conserve my energy and focus.  I can’t review everything and I never could.

When someone directly asks for a review of a large PR, I directly tell them it’s too large.  I explain that it takes a lot of time to review something so big.  I have a strong standard for both PR diff and descriptions.

Saying “no” works if you give people tools to get to “yes”.

Stacked PRs are a wonderful tool to break up large PRs, and LLMs are quite wonderful at doing most of the splitting.  They are mediocre at figuring out good ways to split, sadly.  So if someone is interested in learning, I directly teach them how I would split a large PR.  There’s a lot of taste and not a lot of good rules.

I’ve found amazing success with sitting down with people and reviewing with them.  When they see what I’m reviewing for and looking for, they understand better.  I’ll vocalize my questions and concerns as I review, write them down, and cross them off as I review.

I introduced a plain-language skill at my work that works really well.  I usually tell people I couldn’t understand their docs, comments, or PR descriptions without it, so I require they apply it to their code before approval.

By doing the above, I usually can break apart the review into chunks of questionable material.  Those chunks are the smaller PRs.  If it were actually smaller PRs, I would have quickly found answers to my questions like “was this a move or a refactor”.

LLM code reviews are useful, but only if you have taste.  It flags EVERYTHING and you have to have judgement of what is worth fixing and what is a hallucination.  Here, you say no to the LLM, and it’s often quite receptive.  I’ll literally say no to it with reason, and sometimes it’ll correctly push back with something I missed.

Finally, I really struggle with how some people speak these days, they have their own dialect of LLM in their voice.  So I usually work with an LLM: give it context, quote the person, ask the LLM for a plain language version, and ask my paraphrase is correct.  I go back and forth until it feels clear.  For these folks, communication is not their strength, so I try to meet them where they are and push them to improve in other ways.

comments.author: pyj
comments.text:
Set boundaries and say “no”, with ways to get to “yes”.

When they see what I’m reviewing for and looking for, they understand better.


This shows how you're trying to ensure quality and not just be a roadblock.

Teammembers might also be able to codify some things in their AGENTS.md files or in skills so you can prevent things from making it to review. If the best you can do is getting folks to talk about what they review, just standardizing the team on quality aspects is a win.

comments.author: pyj
comments.text:
If there isn't a good summary written of "Why?" and "What?" with the PR, it's an immediate "return to sender." A PR shouldn't chuck work over the wall and force you to reverse engineer it.  It should be an engineering demonstration of "This is what we needed, this is what I considered, here's the code and why it works." If you allow otherwise, these sort of extensive reviews will tank your productivity and you'll be dealing with those consequences while the "productive" people get the kudos.

A lot of review systems let people stack up multiple reviews in sequence. I would ask them to limit the size of PRs and work in atomic units, and if they don't and still send massive ones just send them back.

In parallel to my review, I'd kick off an AI review with one from a set of prompts I'd been curating. When I'm done reviewing, I'd check what AI says. I split out the files in the review tree, get a feel for the overall, and then tackle the simple leaf parts first.

Code reviews are a two way street, don't approve what you aren't comfortable with. Add lots of comments where appropriate and feel OK saying "Changes are required."

comments.author: jackklika
comments.text: This is where we are moving too - LLM generated PRs are ok, and even sending a Claude response in an answer to a question on slack is ok, but the author needs to include human-typed text and thoughts at the top to give a "why" and "what" which describes the human intent and rationale. The agent responses are artifacts or attachments to the author's intent, not the entire answer. And more importantly the author should be available to voice chat or respond to these questions.

comments.author: pyj
comments.text:
sending a Claude response in an answer to a question on slack is ok


That sounds dystopian and like an easy way to drop the ball on engineering communication. I'm asking probably because I've already looked and also asked an LLM.

comments.author: jackklika
comments.text:
Sometimes it is a cross team thing where the person asking the question may not have the context - in multiple senses - of what they are looking for.

For example let's say I'm responsible for infra spend, and find some lambda that is costing us money but doesn't seem to be working, I can have the agent dig into this and give a timeline of when it was provisioned / what the errors are / how much it is costing. Then when bringing this up to the person who may have provisioned the lambda, I can explain what led to me finding this, and then paste the agent findings at the bottom of the message for them to read.

The Claude output is not the full answer, but an artifact on the message. Like if I pasted a csv snippet or code snippet.

But you are right that it could be considered a failing of the engineering org that the question asker's agent does not have this context, and sometimes a failing of the asker for not doing enough work to answer it themselves.

comments.author: pyj
comments.text:
That makes sense, thanks for the clarification! Your original phrasing made it sound like the answerer was just having the LLM answer. This sounds more like posting a link to a stack dump or troubleshooting log when asking the question, like "Here's how I got here."

Do you also submit the prompt? I'm curious since there doesn't seem to be parity between how different people usage of LLMs.

comments.author: jackklika

comments.author: chipx86
comments.text:
(For context: I founded Review Board, one of the earliest code and doc review products on the market — 20 years now — and have been building that and thinking about these problems for a while, so... I have opinions. But I'll keep it simple.)

I'm in full agreement, a 6K line diff is too much for a human to review, and AI-only review isn't the answer. I've been fighting the "please break your changes into smaller pieces" uphill battle for two decades, and I think it's been hard partly because it's a lot of work to retroactively break up a change and it requires a different mentality when you're actually doing the coding work.

AIs aren't making that any easier for humans, between large diffs and larger influxes of changes and progressively less and less context forming in anyone's heads.

I've been spending a lot of time thinking and working on this problem lately. I do think there's a lot that can/needs to be done here for review and retaining institutional knowledge beyond just giving up and giving in to AIs. But, fighting fire with fire, I do think AI tooling (as part of a broader strategy and toolset) can help with this problem in a way that still keeps the human firmly in control and informed.

Our space is very saturated now, so I'm keeping some of what we're building for this close to the chest until we're ready to announce, but one thing you might consider is using AI to help you break things down locally so you can focus on smaller pieces at a time. Should help you see what's going on and fit more of it in your own head.

You can also try to start by having AI do a first pass and summarize at a higher level what the change is trying to do and where to start with your review process, what things you should know and remember and focus on and look out for, rather than just "please review this (so another AI can fix it)."

(Or wire up an agent to check for diff sizes and complexity and reply with helpful prompts the developer can add to their CLAUDE.md to better cap commits, every single time they do it... Let me know how that works out for you.)

I believe more code review tools need to let teams set limits on diff sizes, too. That's one of the things we offer, but increasingly something that companies turn off due to pressure from developers producing large diffs. It's at least a first stab at encouraging people to be mindful of diff sizes.

There's also a lot of good discussion in this thread. Things are messy right now and a lot of us are seeing the same problems, with very few really good solutions. I'm hoping I can bring some fresh approaches to the market (I really think there's a lot that a dedicated and well-integrated code review tool can do here, if it's wired in right.), but I also think our industry's going to be learning some hard lessons here soon about combining cognitive debt with "move even faster and break even more things".

comments.author: faassen
comments.text:
I know the dogma is that you have issue as the first moment to collaborate, then coding happens, and then a PR appears and that's the second and last moment of collaboration (and often the first one between developers).

Developers like it as they don't have to bother with anyone else, can work autonomously, can feel productive. Organizations like it as it's legible and they can pretend developers are always replaceable with other developers without affecting the quality of the outcome.

But you could talk to each other, work on stuff together, along the way build theories together about how things work now and how they should work, and keep all this in the back of your head as you work on new features. This, I think, results in a higher quality system in the end, and also important, people are happier too. But it takes time and effort and needs to be supported. Intense collaboration isn't easy.

Who knows whether this is really the case anymore with AI development. We're all finding our way in this and the situation keeps evolving. My intuition is that quality still requires human understanding. That human understanding is more important the more novel your project is, and the more critical a piece of infrastructure it is. That AI lets you run ahead of your human understanding (just like using someone else's library or programming language is), but that if you run ahead too far you get into trouble. But again, we're in unprecedented times here.

A 6K diff hitting you is a management issue. Humans will always be overwhelmed by the speed of automation (genAI or not) - in other branches of engineering, like manufacturing, humans are allowed to access samples to establish quality and only rarely they are expected to check every single output. The answer to your question is that, you don't handle a 6K lines diff. It doesn't mean that these 6K lines diff won't need to be verified somehow, and we could discuss what technologies and techniques can be used for the verification but I believe it is out of the scope of the OP's question.

And more subtle management mistake also in play, it seems: the non-crisp separation of Ai-driven coding and human driven coding. For good or for bad, people who decided to not read the code and handed coding to AI shouldn't share the same playground of coding artisans. They cannot co-exist - and often the artisan will simply loathe the AI-pilled folks. Makes no sense using the "be professional" card on people that will so obviously antagonize one another.

So the fact the you put yourself or that someone put you in the path of an automated coding flow is an indication of an organizational problem.

Some, namely artisans, will claim your workplace is broken if you aren't allowed to pull the andon cord and block a 6K diff. Maybe that's the case, but you also have to ask yourself if you're not out of place, in being in a company that decided to give up on their code crafting ways. It is possible and likely that a PR with a 6K diff is the intended goal here.

comments.author: kornel
comments.text:
AI producing the code diarrhoea is not compatible with the current review workflows we have. I don't think both can survive in their current form.

Some partial mitigations require throwing more AI at the AI:




You can tell AI to split the changes into smaller PRs. You can try nagging it to write DRY code and challenge it to redo the change in half of the lines of code (BTW don't try to salvage any existing code. AI is better at rewriting from scratch than editing code).




Set up AI code review, run all the linters you can find, give it checklists to follow, make it try hard to prove the code has bugs.




You can tell AI to write you a walkthrough of the changes, and tune the prompt to exclude stuff you already know. Require the doc to be logically structured, and force it through a few rounds of removing verbosity.

comments.author: gkoos
comments.text:
We accidentally ran a small experiment with AI-assisted code review at work.
I was working on a fairly underspecified ticket and needed a PR approval to merge to main. The only colleague available was working on a different part of the project and didn't have much context on what I was changing.
They normally use a bespoke AI agent to assist with their own reviews, where they know the code and can properly judge its suggestions. In this case, though, they admittedly relied much more heavily on the agent and only superficially triaged its comments.
The first review round was actually useful. It caught a couple of edge cases and made some reasonable suggestions.
The second round was mostly nitpicking, but I made the suggested changes anyway.
By the third round, it was proposing changes that effectively reverted changes it had asked for in the second round.
At that point we stopped, because it became fairly obvious that it wasn't converging toward "this is good enough, approve". It would apparently just keep finding something to comment on.
A human reviewer has an implicit stopping condition: the code doesn't have to be exactly how they would have written it; it has to be good enough to merge. An LLM prompted to review a PR seems to have no equivalent concept unless the human supervising it supplies one.
Once it has exhausted the meaningful issues, it won't just say "looks good". It can move on to subjective preferences, increasingly marginal suggestions, and eventually contradict its own previous advice, so the problem not just humans reviewing LLM-written code, LLM reviewing human-written code is not much better :D

comments.author: mordae
comments.text:
I don't care about the nits as much anymore. Apart for big-O fuckups that pop up in random places occasionally. Having junior colleagues and deadlines forced me not to care as much.

What's an actual problem is when the commit completely reinvents the architecture and does its own thing.

This happens when a clueless junior vibe codes because seniors are bottlecked or merely when we (seniors and juniors) are stretched thin and someone has to step into a project they are not that familiar with. With a deadline.

So far the best course of action, it seems, is not being passive aggressive, but understanding and mutual support. Telling others reviewing 6kloc diff on the core logic on a friday afternoon is impossible. Noting the biggest problems you can spot to unblock the process. Postponing detailed review to next week, after the biggest problems have been addressed. And discussing how did the agent miss them, working out ways to prevent that in the future.

And most importantly: discussing the overall architecture and plans with the actual human.

Disclaimer: I work with a team that gets hired for various projects. We are not on a long-term corporate payroll. We all want to deliver.

comments.text:
I'm not sure breaking it down into smaller PRs (as the common advice here suggests) will help. I frequently have asked AI agents to break a change into smaller commits or stacked PRs. It will oblige, but the smaller PRs are not that much easier to review in isolation IMHO.

Personally, I find AI code exhausting to review. Far more exhausting than reviewing human code. I'm not yet sure why. Personally I've gotten better at quickly reading large AI PRs, and I find it preferable to reviewing many smaller AI diffs. It's hard to evaluate them with the same scrutiny, but I find when agents go wrong, it's quite wrong as a matter of design, so you can get a good feeling for how reliable it is fairly quickly.

I'd also ask PR authors to remove useless AI comments, which reduces the LOC dramatically. I then collapse all testcases initially - because AI tests can be a blovation - and try to understand the code logic first.

Whether this works for you will depend on how big your codebase is, how critical your industry, what part of the codebase you're contributing to, etc.

[For some context, pre-AI I also preferred to review and create small <400 line PRs, and often preferred to read the testcases first to get a sense of the intended behaviour change. So the above is a fairly different workflow to what I'm used to.]

comments.author: olliej
comments.text:
First up: reject any PR like this - require that they split it up.

Require every review include a report of the time spent reviewing.

Require that they confirm that they have reviewed the AI changes, as if it was written by a [drunk?] junior engineer, prior to asking for your review, and that the review process be on the PR, in whatever your standard review system is. That way there is a record of issues that they found and fixed during the final review they did before asking for a secondary review. Again, the review must include time spent.

Spend the time they claimed to have spent reviewing the PR, reviewing the PR. If you are nowhere near completing the review, ask how they reviewed the code so quickly. If you find yourself repeatedly encountering the myriad obvious LLM code issues: symptom suppression rather than fixes, duplicated code, duplicated helper functions, single use single expression helpers, different ways to do the same thing, wildly unnecessary comments, etc, the simply stop, and ask them to actually do a review of the code.

Do not allow them to waste your time with PRs that even they are unwilling to review, and frankly make it clear that this is a core part of using an AI: if you did not write the code, you do not know what it does, and have to review it as such before asking for secondary review.

Also, while depressing: LLMs are actually reasonably good at finding bugs in PRs, so you could simply ask whatever one you're expected to use to search for bugs - I've spent a bunch of time constructing various "skills", "workflows", or whatever the nonsense is being called today with the explicit intent of forcing the LLM to do an adversarial review: e.g. assume the code is broken, assume that the breakage may not be local, etc, verify any discovered breakage, etc - make sure whatever you're writing to the chatbot also knows about common slop idioms (duplicate code, unnecessary helpers, dead code, etc).

To be clear: I actually did this for my own code changes, because reasoning about edge cases is miserable, and just kept expanding it when my own reviews found things it missed.

The other benefit of this is that your management will see you are doing the all important task of burning trees, a task much more important than your actual job.

comments.author: smaddox
comments.text:
6k diff average is pretty crazy, but I've certainly seen prior norms for PR size balloon, and I've been guilty myself.

That being said, I no longer find the need to do very tedious fine-grained reviews, checking for all the fine details that humans get wrong, because LLM's are super human at so much of the fine-grained details. As long as I know a competent LLM was used, or I've had a competent LLM review the fine-grained details, that frees me up to think bigger picture.

Although, TBF, with the pace of code development, there's still more big picture tech debt accumulation than I think is healthy, and more than would be practical pre LLM's, so development velocity of larger requirements changes / new features seems to slow to the same crawl it did pre-LLMs. Which is, I think, why we haven't seen an explosion in productivity in anything outside of small greenfield projects.

But LLM's continue getting better. They're already better than most of the engineers I've worked with. And they're better than me in several aspects, certainly in terms of speed of going from concept to implementation.

I can sympathize with disdain about LLM-based development. It removes most of the enjoyable aspects of the job, at least for me, at least for any project involving more than a single developer.

Unfortunately, given the rate of improvement of these models, I think rejecting LLM-based software development entirely will prove to be not dissimilar from being a Luddite.

I don't know what the future holds for this profession, but however it evolves, I plan to remain at the forefront as well as I can. That doesn't mean I'm ready to stop looking at the code completely, but it does mean I'm continuing to explore the capabilities of these models and leverage them as effectively as I can, while still producing as high-quality software as the organization(s) I'm working in are able and willing to produce.

My previous employer was hyper-aggressive about submitting PRs which were split into individual atomic commits, split semantically ("each individual commit tells a story"). It sucked to produce but did make reviewing much easier. I've found that LLMs are pretty good at doing this split, and that work is trivially verifiable (do a git diff between the before and after commit). You might want to write a skill for your coworkers and refuse to review PRs unless they use it -- if you phrase it well, you can make it look like a new toy instead of a new burden.
